pois.name: Takeshita Street
pois.description: The iconic pedestrian street of Harajuku — 400m of crepe stands, vintage shops, and street fashion. Peak chaos on weekends when cosplayers and rockabilly dancers take over.

pois.name: Meiji Shrine
pois.description: Shinto shrine dedicated to Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken (1920). The 100-year-old forest of 100,000 trees was donated by the Japanese people. Massive torii gates mark the entrance.

350-metre pedestrian street — Tokyo's epicentre of Harajuku street fashion, cosplay, and youth culture since the 1980s. Peak on Sundays: over 200,000 visitors. Crepe stands, gothic-lolita boutiques, and streetwear pop-ups line every metre.

pois.name: Meiji Jingu Shrine
pois.description: Shinto shrine (1920) dedicated to Emperor Meiji and Empress Shoken, set in 70 hectares of forest. The towering wooden torii gate is one of Japan's largest — 12 metres high, built from 1,500-year-old Taiwanese cypress. Sees 3 million visitors in the three days of New Year's.

pois.name: Yoyogi Park
pois.description: 54-hectare park in the heart of Tokyo. Cherry blossoms in spring, maple leaves in autumn. Weekends see rockabilly dancers near the entrance and drum circles near the pond.

54-hectare urban park, former 1964 Olympic Village. Cherry blossoms (hanami) in April draw half a million visitors. Rockabilly dancers and street musicians perform at the main gate on Sundays — a Tokyo Sunday ritual since the 1980s.

pois.name: Omotesando Avenue
pois.description: Tokyo's Champs-Élysées — 1km zelkova-tree-lined boulevard leading to Meiji Shrine. Flagship stores: Prada, Dior, Omotesando Hills (Tadao Ando, 2006).

pois.name: Togo Shrine
pois.description: Small but popular Shinto shrine dedicated to Admiral Togo Heihachiro (victor of the 1905 Battle of Tsushima). Famous for matchmaking and maritime blessings.

pois.name: Ura-Harajuku
pois.description: The backstreets of Harajuku — Cat Street and the lanes between Omotesando and Shibuya. Independent boutiques, craft cafes, and street art. Less crowded than Takeshita.

name: Omotesando
description: Tokyo's most prestigious shopping boulevard — a zelkova-tree-lined avenue flanked by architecturally significant flagships: Prada (Herzog & de Meuron), Louis Vuitton (Jun Aoki), Dior, and Omotesando Hills (Tadao Ando, 2006). Often called 'Tokyo's Champs-Élysées'.

partnerURL.name: Harajuku Station
partnerURL.description: A small wooden JR station (original 1906 building preserved) wedged between Meiji Jingu forest and Takeshita Street. One of Tokyo's most charming and historically intact station buildings — contrasting sharply with the youth-culture explosion just outside its gates.
